title: Inflation & real returns
examples: How much does inflation really affect my savings?
What is the difference between nominal and real interest rates?
If I earn 5 percent but inflation is 3 percent, what is my real gain?

explain.say: Today we look at real versus nominal returns.

items: Nominal Return: The stated rate of return.
Real Return: The return adjusted for inflation.

explain.say: Nominal return is simply the number you see quoted.
Inflation measures how much prices are rising overall.
The real return shows your actual buying power change.
To find the real return, you subtract inflation from the nominal return.
Consider saving one hundred dollars today and it becomes one hundred five dollars next year.

faq.q: What is the best way to calculate the real return?
faq.a: The most accurate way is to use the formula involving the minus sign. A simpler estimate is to subtract inflation from the nominal rate.
asks: How do I adjust for inflation?
Is there a formula for real return?

faq.q: Does the real return only matter for long-term investments?
faq.a: No, it matters for any time period where prices might change. Even short-term savings are affected by inflation.
asks: When should I worry about real returns?

faq.q: If the nominal return is less than inflation, what happens?
faq.a: If the nominal return is less than inflation, your real return is negative. This means your money buys less than it did before.
asks: What does a negative real return mean?

faq.q: Is the simple subtraction method always accurate enough?
faq.a: It is a good quick estimate, but for precision, you should use the full formula involving the minus sign. The simple subtraction can overestimate the true loss.
asks: Is subtraction okay for real returns?

faq.q: What causes inflation to change over time?
faq.a: Inflation is caused by a general rise in the price level of goods and services. This can be due to increased demand or supply issues.
asks: Why do prices keep going up?

facts: Nominal return is the stated rate of return without adjusting for inflation.
Inflation is the rate at which the general level of prices for goods and services rises.
A negative real return means your purchasing power has decreased.
The real return tells you the actual change in your standard of living.

quiz.say: A bond yields 4 percent nominally, and the inflation rate is 2 percent. What is the approximate real return?
quiz.why: You subtract the inflation rate from the nominal rate to find the approximate real return, which is 2 percent.

wrong.0: Adding the rates together suggests the gains are compounding, which is incorrect for this simple comparison.
wrong.1: This assumes that inflation cancels out all gains, which is only true if the rates are equal.
wrong.2: Dividing the inflation by two is an arbitrary adjustment that has no basis in economic calculation.

quiz.say: If your savings earn 1 percent, but inflation is 3 percent, what is your real return?
quiz.why: Since inflation (3 percent) is higher than your gain (1 percent), your money loses purchasing power, resulting in a negative real return.

wrong.1: This incorrectly calculates the difference as a positive gain, ignoring the loss of value.
wrong.2: This only states the nominal return and fails to account for the erosion of value due to rising prices.
wrong.3: This incorrectly uses the inflation rate as the final answer, ignoring the initial investment gain.

quiz.say: Which scenario results in a positive real return?

options.show: Nominal return must be greater than inflation.
options.say: Nominal return must be greater than inflation.

quiz.why: For your actual buying power to increase, the rate you earn must exceed the rate at which prices are rising.

wrong.0: While timing matters, the fundamental condition for a positive real return is the relationship between the two rates, not just the year.
wrong.2: If they are equal, the real return is zero, meaning no actual gain in purchasing power.
wrong.3: If the nominal rate is lower, the real return will be negative, meaning you are losing value.
